scenes.text: Last time, nine skills that protect health. Now we turn them on you. Write down one thing you'd change about your own health, if changing it were free and instant. Then write the reason you haven't. Now look at that reason. Is it about your choices, or about your circumstances? Most people write one and mean the other.

The syllabus asks you to reflect on your own health, and that word invites a diary entry. But reflection is a method: a structured review that ends in a conclusion and a change. If nothing you do next is different, you described, you didn't reflect. It has four steps. Describe what's actually happening, in specifics: not I sleep badly, but in bed by eleven, asleep near one, four nights in seven. Analyse why: is it a behaviour, a condition, or a coping strategy doing a job for you? Conclude something you didn't know at the start. Then plan a specific next action, with a date to review it.

And reflection isn't self-criticism. Self-criticism ends in a judgement about the person: I've got no discipline. That produces shame, and no action. Reflection ends in a judgement about a situation: my phone charges beside my bed, and at eleven I check it. That produces an action so small it's almost embarrassing. Move the charger. It's the same argument as resilience: putting the problem inside the person explains nothing.

To describe yourself well, run a self-audit across the dimensions of health, physical, mental and social. For each, write what's true now, and the evidence. I'm not fit is an impression. I've trained twice in three weeks is evidence, and it's the one you can act on. Count something, nights, sessions, meals, so you have a baseline to compare against later. Watch how dimensions interact, and include what's going well. And an audit isn't a diagnosis. If it turns up something that worries you, that's a moment for help-seeking, not a workbook.

Now the key step, the agency boundary. Sort every item into three columns. Yours to change now, like when the phone goes down. Yours to influence, like asking for a lift on training nights, or joining something. And not yours, like household income, local transport, or whether the club exists at all. Students go wrong in both directions. Put a column-one item in column three, and your plan becomes a complaint. Put a column-three item in column one, and it becomes self-blame with a deadline. If there's no food in the house on Thursdays, no amount of intention fixes Thursday.

Column three isn't where you give up. Naming a condition accurately lets you do two useful things. Work around it, with a different day, a cheaper option or a free service. Or take it to someone whose job it is to change it, which is where advocacy begins. A condition you've named can be raised with someone. One you've mislabelled as a personal failing can't.

Then write the course of action, and make it usable, with five properties. Specific: walk from the second-last stop, not get fitter. Small: one session on Wednesday, not five days a week from Monday. Scheduled: four pm, in the calendar. Supported: one person knows and is expecting you, which recruits connectedness. And reviewable: judged on a set date against your starting count. Small is the one people drop, because it feels like not trying. But a small action done eleven times out of fourteen changes a baseline, and a big one done twice changes nothing but your opinion of yourself.

Even then, many people who intend to sleep more or move more don't. In exercise studies, close to half of people who intend to move more don't follow through. That distance is the intention-behaviour gap, and a plan should expect it. Attach the action to a moment you already meet: when the ten thirty alarm goes, the phone goes on the desk. Write the bad-week version now, fifteen minutes instead of a session, so a bad week costs one session, not the whole plan. And if the old habit was doing a job, plan what replaces it. A missed day is data, not a verdict, and the review date is where you adjust.
Two things to remember. Reflection ends in a change, not a feeling. And draw the boundary before you plan: change what's yours, and name what isn't.

Two exam questions. First. A student writes, I never eat breakfast because I'm lazy. From Monday I'll eat a healthy breakfast every single day. Identify two weaknesses in this reflection, and rewrite it as a usable course of action. Pause here to answer.

First weakness: it's self-criticism, with no evidence or analysis. Second: the plan is big, with no cue and no review date. A usable version: on school days, when I fill my water bottle at seven fifteen, I take a banana and a yoghurt, my family keeps them stocked, and I review in three weeks. The classic mistake is changing the target and nothing else.
Second. Assess the value of personal reflection as a way of improving the health of young people. Pause here to answer.

Judge it with a boundary. For: it turns impressions into evidence, it's free, and it builds skills like self-efficacy. Against: it can name a condition precisely, but can't change it, and if it's sold as enough, a failed plan feels like personal failure. So it's valuable within your own agency, and what it finds in column three feeds advocacy. The classic mistake is calling it quite useful, with no boundary.

So, describe with evidence, draw the boundary, and write a small plan built for a bad week. Now check the reason you wrote at the start: a choice, or a condition? Next, column three. How have young people changed the conditions themselves?
